definition: Haikubox is an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled device which automatically and continuously identifies backyard birds using their vocalizations.
details: Haikubox was developed by Loggerhead Instruments which also develops and manufactures bioacoustics equipment for oceanographic research. Haikubox uses a neural net developed through a collaboration with the creators of BirdNET Sound ID at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics. Each Haikubox becomes a node in a passive acoustic monitoring (PAM) network which researchers can use to map bird behavior. PAM, especially when paired with machine learning, is emerging as an efficient, non-invasive and low-cost way to study animals and their behavioral responses to environmental change. As of January 1, 2025, over one billion bird recordings have been captured by Haikuboxes. Haikubox data was used to study the April 8, 2024 total solar eclipse that crossed North America, and the peer-reviewed findings were published in Scientific Reports. The study found that at locations experiencing more than 99 percent obscurity, and in the absence of human vocalizations, birds generally stopped vocalizing, but that there was variability between locations and individual species responses. explainer.lead: Haikubox is a listening device that automatically identifies backyard birds from their songs and calls. Because many units can operate continuously as a connected monitoring network, they can reveal bird activity and behavior without researchers having to watch every location.

tiers.eli5: Haikubox is like a music-recognition app for birds: it listens to their sounds and works out which bird is making them. Lots of these listeners can work together, helping scientists notice patterns that would be hard to spot from one backyard. During the 2024 total solar eclipse, for example, birds at very dark locations generally became quiet.
tiers.practitioner: Haikubox is deployed as a continuously operating passive acoustic monitoring node, with its neural network turning bird vocalizations into identifications that researchers can aggregate across locations. It is useful for long-running, non-invasive behavioral studies, but analyses should account for variation among sites and species. The eclipse study also shows why potentially confounding sounds, such as human vocalizations, need attention.
tiers.paperLevel: Haikubox can be represented as a continuous passive-acoustic sensor: an audio stream is processed by a neural network for bird sound identification, and each device contributes observations to a distributed PAM network. Its neural net was developed through collaboration with the creators of BirdNET Sound ID at the Cornell Lab of Ornithology's K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics. A Scientific Reports study of the April 8, 2024 eclipse found generally reduced vocalization at locations above 99 percent obscurity when human vocalizations were absent, while emphasizing location- and species-specific variability.

explainer.example: Haikubox data was used to study the total solar eclipse that crossed North America on April 8, 2024. At locations with more than 99 percent obscurity and no human vocalizations, birds generally stopped vocalizing, although responses varied by location and species; the peer-reviewed findings appeared in Scientific Reports.

explainer.intuition: Many birds are easier to hear than to see, so continuous listening can provide a practical record of their presence and activity. Linking many automatic listeners turns individual backyard observations into a broader picture of bird behavior.
howItWorks: A Haikubox continuously captures bird vocalizations in its surroundings.
Its neural network analyzes the sounds to identify the birds.
Each device operates as a node in a passive acoustic monitoring network.
Researchers use the combined data to map bird behavior and study responses to environmental change.
explainer.whyItMatters: Continuous, automated listening makes bird monitoring non-invasive and relatively low-cost, allowing observations at a scale that manual surveys cannot easily match. The resulting data can reveal both broad behavioral patterns and important differences between places and species.
misconceptions: It does not identify birds from photographs or video; it listens to their vocalizations.
It is not simply an isolated backyard identifier: each unit can also contribute to a research monitoring network.
Its eclipse result was not a universal rule for every bird, since responses varied among locations and species.
